newsitem.title: USA: Race a key issue in Southern Senate campaigns.
newsitem.headline: Race a key issue in Southern Senate campaigns.

text.p: Whether the Republican Party retains control of the U.S. Senate this November is a question that could depend on where Southern voters come down on the hot-button issue of race, analysts and politicians say.
Charges of race-baiting have erupted between Republican Jeff Sessions and Democrat Roger Bedford in Alabama, where opinion polls show voters starkly divided along racial lines.

In Louisiana white Democratic Senate candidate Mary Landrieu faces a potential boycott by black political leaders that would doom her chances in a close fight against hardline Republican conservative Woody Jenkins.
And, in Georgia, a double-digit lead for Democrat Max Cleland came on the heels of revelations about Republican Guy Millner's membership in a Florida country club known for excluding blacks and Jews.
"The big issue is the racial issue," said Charles Hadley, a political scientist at the University of New Orleans.
Republicans are trying to upend a Democratic challenge for Senate control by using the South as a hedge against potential losses in other parts of the country.
Republicans hold a 53-47 advantage in the chamber. But a net gain of three seats would give Democrats the edge with Vice President Al Gore holding the tie-breaking vote.

At stake in the South are open seats in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia and Louisiana, where Democratic incumbents are stepping down after decades of control. Analysts say Republicans need to pick up at least two of them to head off the Democrats and secure their position in the Senate.
"These are all competitive races. We could go from the extremes of four Democratic gains, I think, to four Republican gains," said Rice University political scientist Earl Black.
Race has become a major issue in two states where likely victory margins of only a few percentage points seem to depend less on the presidential campaign.
"There are two things that motivate voters in Alabama: race and fear," said a senior aide to a ranking Democrat in the state House of Representatives.
A recent Alabama poll gave Sessions, the Republican attorney general, a nine-point lead over Bedford in a contest marked by increasing polarisation along racial lines.

"About 60 percent of white voters are supporting the Republican candidate. In the past it's been more like 50 percent," said William Stewart, a political science professor at the University of Alabama.

Bedford later charged Sessions with using the race card in a radio ad that played on the support he received from prominent black leaders. "Here we are, trying to move Alabama forward into the 21st Century and he's going back to the way things were in the 1950s," said Bedford, a state Senator.

A Sessions spokesman later dismissed the charge, saying the ad underscored support for Bedford from several noted liberals, including Massachusettes Sen. Ted Kennedy and former Vice President Walter Mondale.

But local politicians say Sessions has gained stature among white voters since his confrontation in the 1980s with Reagan Republicans in the Senate, who blocked his appointment to a federal judgeship for allegedly making racist remarks. "Those wouldn't necessarily be problems in Alabama," said one analyst.

Analysts say the race card in Louisiana is being played by supporters of black U.S. Representative Cleo Fields who are feuding with Landrieu, a former Democratic state treasurer, because of her failure to support Fields in the last gubernatorial race.

Meanwhile, Jenkins, a Republican who has been dubbed "David Duke Lite" for his staunch conservative views, has drawn support from 15 percent of the black voters, mostly Christian conservatives attracted by his opposition to abortion.
"We figure Mary needs 99 percent of the African vote in a big voter turnout, plus 35 percent of the white vote," said Landrieu spokesman Rick Masters.

The latest opinion poll in Georgia showed Democrat Cleland with a comfortable 16-point lead over Millner. A month ago, a poll showed him leading the Republican by 12 points. In the interim, Millner, who lost his 1994 bid for governor, has been forced to surrender an eight-year membership in the Everglades Club of Palm Beach, Florida, a resort described by the American Jewish Congress as a "notorious discriminator" for barring blacks and Jews.
Millner campaign officials dismissed the poll results and his club membership. But analysts believe his club membership may have energised Cleland's standing among moderate voters.

"Most Georgians have made up their minds, especially after the revelation on the other side that this gentleman was a member of a club that excluded about 40 percent of Georgia while running for governor and the U.S. Senate," Cleland said.
